tier_reason: The Benchmarks page does print ALR-vs-gRPC tables (localhost 1 thread: 3,761,550 vs 34,386; 3,614,312 vs 37,089; 14,288,968 vs 42,671 RPC/s). But the page calls them 'illustrative summaries based on previously gathered runs', and DISCLAIMER.md calls the performance numbers 'forward-looking' and says not to rely on them. There is no benchmark code, gRPC client/server code, gRPC version, API mode, in-flight depth, compiler or flags, and no library source, so the ~97-335x figures cannot be traced to a real measurement. They are treated as no usable numbers (D).

corrections.benchmark_url: https://atomiclinkrpc.github.io/alr-preview/benchmarks/ (source: https://github.com/AtomicLinkRPC/alr-preview/blob/main/docs/benchmarks.md). The 'Raw Results' pages are ALR-only: 'a different set of tests than the ALR vs. gRPC tests'.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Page (self-described as 'illustrative'), localhost 1 thread: RoundTripStringAsyncCB 3,761,550 vs gRPC 34,386 RPC/s (~109x, derived from page data); RoundTripSmallMsgAsyncCB 3,614,312 vs 37,089 (~97x, derived); StreamSmallMsgFromServer 14,288,968 vs 42,671 (~335x, derived). Localhost 100 threads: RoundTripStringAsyncCB 16,040,522 vs 245,336 (~65x, derived); StreamSmallMsgFromServer 65,472,788 vs 392,855 (~167x, derived). Across all 100-thread localhost tests ALR ranges 63,107-65,472,788 and gRPC 1,531-392,855 RPC/s, not the '16.0M-65.5M vs 245K-393K' range in the record.
corrections.license: CC-BY-4.0 (documentation only, per LICENSE-DOCS.md; no source code published, so no code licence)
corrections.caveats: Docs-only preview with no framework source (README: 'Framework source code. This preview is docs-only'; HN post: 'The source is not public yet'). The Benchmarks page calls its numbers 'illustrative summaries based on previously gathered runs', and DISCLAIMER.md says the performance numbers are forward-looking and should not be relied on. Only the gRPC proto definitions and message-fill snippets are shown; the gRPC client/server code, gRPC version, sync/async/callback mode, outstanding-request depth, compiler and flags are not. ALR 'AsyncCB' runs use opportunistic batching (the raw logs show average batches of hundreds to thousands of messages per socket write), while gRPC 1-thread rates of ~34-42K RPC/s look like one request in flight at a time, so the comparison is likely not like-for-like. The gRPC RoundTripStringAsyncCB 1-thread figure (34,386) is identical in the localhost and 2.5GbE-remote tables, which suggests a copy error. Roadmap lists 'v0.2 Public demos & perf harness' as future work. 0 stars, 0 issues; Ask HN (id 45173846) has 3 points and 0 comments.

tier_reason: The README Benchmark table compares exposed and grpc head-to-head across 75 paired configurations and states the CPU (i7-7700HQ). The gRPC comparison harness is not in the repo; server_timing_test.go benchmarks only exposed itself. The Go version and flags are not stated. That makes this first-party with partial methodology: tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table, 8-byte payload, 1 client, concurrency 50: exposed 527,199.3 op/s vs grpc 394,620.7 op/s (~1.34x, derived from page data); total memory allocated 472 MB vs 1.4 GB; GC count 111 vs 538. Best mid-size case: 8B, 5 clients, concurrency 5000: 1,003,451.8 vs 329,039.9 op/s (~3.0x, derived). gRPC is faster in some rows (8B/10 clients/concurrency 50 and 500; 128B/10/50 and 500; 32768B/1/5000). The README has no prose claim of winning across nearly all scenarios; that is a reading of the table. Rows at 32K/64K payload with concurrency 50000 show gRPC at ~0 op/s (failed runs), so ratios from those rows are meaningless.
corrections.workload: Echo-style RPC round trips, server and client on the same machine; payload 8/128/1024/32768/65536 bytes x 1/5/10 clients x concurrency 1/50/500/5000/50000 (as labelled in the README); reports op/s, MB/s, p50/p95/p99/max latency, GC count and total memory allocated.

corrections.caveats: Abandoned: last commit 2018-08-02. The gRPC comparison harness is not published; the repo's server_timing_test.go only benchmarks exposed end-to-end.
